definition: The difficulty a person has in putting something they hold internally — an intent, a felt reaction, a quality criterion, a piece of advice — into an explicit form another party can act on. The person is taken to know, at some level, what they want; the claimed problem is the conversion into words, parameters, or a stated principle. It is a difficulty of expression, not of deciding.
framing: DEFICIT/HARM. The corpus names it as a difficulty, a burden of conversion, or a "not straightforward" task. A minority of assertions state the complementary capacity in recognition terms (helping a person notice rather than generate), but the framing is still built on the stated difficulty.

definition: The person does not hold a fully formed goal at the moment they must specify one; what they want is partly constructed, and revised, through the act of working on the task. Papers claim their designs engage the condition in which a target is under-specified at the outset and shifts as the person sees intermediate results. The factor concerns the state of the goal itself, not the difficulty of putting an already-held goal into words.
framing: BOTH — the corpus frames vagueness as a defect of the specification moment ("despite inherently vague, fluid, and evolving intents") and equally as a legitimate developmental process worth protecting (preference construction, problem-solution co-evolution).

definition: Getting from a stated goal to the ordered set of sub-goals or steps that would achieve it, and holding that structure while acting on it. The claimed difficulty is that people cannot break their own objective into separable parts, or cannot sustain long-range planning across the many steps a complex outcome requires. It transplants to any goal too large to be accomplished in one move.

human_factor: implicit expression of attention and intent
definition: While a person works, their behaviour continuously leaks where they are looking and what they are after, without their having stated any of it. The factor is this unspoken behavioural signal — gaze, dwell, pointer movement, or comparable traces — treated as a readable expression of attention and intent rather than as mere input. It concerns what the person conveys without deliberate articulation.

Before anything can be solved, the person has to settle what the problem is — which constraints count, what would qualify as an answer, and where the boundaries of the task lie. The factor is that constitutive act of framing, held apart from and prior to solving. It concerns the formulation of the problem, in any domain where the problem is not given ready-made.

The person's capacity to generate, vary, and explore possibilities of their own, and the value the corpus places on that exploratory activity as an activity. Papers claim designs support idea generation, early-stage exploration, iteration on one's own concepts, and the searching through which discovery is said to happen. The unit is the person's generative activity, not the novelty of any artifact produced.
framing: CAPACITY. Stated as something to support, enable, or preserve — creative writing, rapid ideation, early-stage exploration, "a playground for users to explore".

human_factor: need for external inspiration and examples
definition: The claim that people cannot reliably produce ideas from nothing and must go outside themselves — to references, precedents, or examples — to get moving or to get past a stall. Papers state it as blockage, as the cost of starting from scratch, or as an established practice of consulting outside material. The factor is the dependence on external stimulus, not the quality of ideas eventually produced.
framing: BOTH. The corpus states it as a difficulty (writer's block, the challenge of "conceiving vivid graphical design" from scratch, exploration being costly) and as a positively named human need ("inspiration" as the dimension the system is framed around).

human_factor: iterative rather than linear creative process
definition: Creative work does not run start-to-finish; the person cycles between making, looking around, and reworking, and may re-enter an earlier stage at any point. The factor is this non-linear temporal shape of the person's process, asserted as the proper form of the work rather than as an inefficiency. It concerns how the activity is sequenced, not how much of it there is.

Beyond the particular option in front of them, a person needs a sense of the field of possible options — what else could exist, and how the alternatives are laid out relative to each other. The factor is the person's grasp of that space of possibilities for the problem they face. It concerns a map of what is possible, not the production of any one candidate.

The cost of reaching an acceptable result by repeated attempts because the relation between what the person supplies and what comes back cannot be predicted. Papers frame it as random, laborious, or requiring many candidates before one is usable, and as demanding persistence from the person. It is the iteration itself that is claimed to be burdensome, not the difficulty of any single attempt.
framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Named as a laborious, random, or inefficient process, and as requiring persistence — with a secondary framing of serendipity as the reason many attempts are needed.

definition: The person must satisfy several requirements at once that pull against each other, and every choice of what to include or leave out trades one off against another. The claimed difficulty is the simultaneity: no single requirement is hard, but they cannot all be maximized. It transplants to any selection or composition task governed by more than one binding constraint.

The narrowing of what a person considers or produces as a consequence of what they were shown. Papers frame it as fixation — being captured by an example so the space of options shrinks — and as convergence across people who all draw on the same source, reducing the variety of what a group collectively produces. The claim is about the person's range narrowing, not about any single output being poor.
framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Stated as an undesirable outcome — fixation, focus drift, hindered creativity, diminished diversity of results.

human_factor: tension between precise control and surprise
definition: A person sometimes wants exactly what they specified and sometimes wants to be shown something they would not have specified, and the same encounter cannot fully serve both. The factor is this conflict inside the person's own wants — fidelity to a stated criterion against variety and unexpectedness — which the interface must resolve without knowing which mode the person is in. It is a conflict of goals, not a shortage of control.

Recognizing that a structure in one domain matches a structure in an unrelated one, and carrying it across. Papers frame this as a cognitive capacity people cannot exercise on demand: finding a fitting source is hard, and understanding a retrieved one well enough to build from it is a further difficulty. It transplants to any task solved by importing a structure from elsewhere.

The work left to a person of checking whether something produced for them is correct, adequate, or acceptable before they can use it. Papers frame this as labour that has been displaced rather than removed: producing is cheaper, so checking becomes the bottleneck. The factor is the human checking work, not any property of what generated the output.
framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Named as a burden that "remains on the end-user", as effort "shifted" rather than removed, and as an inability to check when only a final result is shown.

definition: A person must commit to a choice at a particular moment, and whether they hold the information that bears on it at that moment is what is at stake. The factor is the person's capacity to decide on an adequate basis at the point of decision, where the relevant material is otherwise dispersed, absent, or arriving too late to act on. It concerns the act of choosing, not the act of understanding for its own sake.

human_factor: judging whether returned material bears on the need
definition: What the system returns may not be about what the person actually wanted, and the person is left to judge the fit between the two. Papers claim their designs engage the gap between a request and the returned material, and the judgment of relevance the person must exercise over candidates. This is a property of the match, not of the correctness of the content.
framing: BOTH — the corpus frames off-target output as a harm (focus drift, unresolved intent-outcome gaps) and also frames relevance judgment as an activity the person performs over candidates.

definition: The condition in which a person must judge something without a settled or stably applied standard: what counts as good is contested, depends on who is judging, or drifts within one judge over a long session. Papers frame the consequence as judgments that cannot be replicated or defended. It concerns the standard being unclear, not the effort of applying a clear one.
framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Framed as subjectivity, unfairness, narrowness of available measures, and lack of replicability — conditions to be remedied.

definition: People can be moved to false beliefs or unwanted decisions by content that is wrong, fallacious, or engineered to persuade, and they vary in how far they resist it. Papers claim their designs engage this vulnerability and the counterpart capacity to withstand it. The factor is the person's exposure and resistance to persuasive falsehood, whatever the source of that content.
framing: BOTH — the corpus names susceptibility, echo chambers, and damaged public trust as harms, and resistance to misinformation and critical examination of content as capacities to be strengthened.

human_factor: linking information back to its referent
definition: A statement can be perfectly clear on its own terms and still be unusable because the person cannot tell which part of the object it is about. The factor is the interpretive gap the person must close between a piece of information and the thing that information concerns, when the two are presented apart from each other. Papers frame this as a gulf of evaluation to be narrowed rather than as a property of the information itself.

The posture a person takes toward what the system produced — whether they treat it as a candidate to be judged right or wrong, as raw material to build on, or as a constraint or resource to work within. The claimed difficulty is that the output's surface properties push the person into a stance that does not serve the task. It transplants to any setting where a person must decide what kind of thing an automatically produced artifact is to them.

The person receives an answer whose underlying confidence is not visible in the answer's surface form, and must decide how much weight to place on it. The factor is the human's handling of stated or unstated uncertainty — whether a spread of possibilities rather than a single value reaches them, and how their own numerical and probabilistic fluency conditions what they do with it. It is about the recipient's position under uncertainty, not about the mechanism that produces the uncertainty.

human_factor: the person's understanding of how an output was produced
definition: The person's ability to see how a result was arrived at — what was considered, what was discarded, and why this outcome rather than another. Papers frame the absence as under-explanation and the presence as understanding, transparency, or the person being able to relate their own inputs to the outcome. It concerns the derivation of a result, not the subject matter the result is about.
framing: BOTH. The corpus states it as a capacity to be enabled ("understanding and assessment of the recommended items") and as a deficit ("under-explored and under-explained").

definition: What the person believes an automated counterpart is able and unable to do, and how that belief forms and shifts across repeated use. Papers frame the deficit as opacity — the person cannot tell what is achievable, so failures arrive unexpectedly — and the capacity as adaptation, where experience accumulates into workable expectations. It is a belief the person holds, not a documented property of the system.
framing: BOTH. The corpus frames it as a deficit (capability "is opaque to the user", the "Gulf of Envisioning", unexpected failures) and as a capacity (users adapt and build up experience across interactions).

definition: Before or during joint work, the person must form expectations about what an autonomous counterpart will do next, or how it will behave across situations they have not yet encountered, in order to plan their own actions. Papers claim their designs engage this forward-looking prediction problem and the difficulty of getting evidence for it in advance. The concern is future behaviour, not explanation of behaviour already observed.
framing: DEFICIT/HARM — the corpus states this as an inability: feedback on behaviour is unavailable before deployment, behaviour across the input range is hard to understand, and problems surface only when they are expensive.

human_factor: awareness of AI involvement and provenance
definition: Whether the person can tell that a machine was involved at all, what it did, and which parts of what they are looking at came from it. The claimed difficulty is that machine involvement is not perceptible in the artifact or the interaction, so the person cannot attribute origin without being told. It applies wherever an output's authorship or generation history bears on how a person should treat it.

The person's willingness to credit an automated counterpart and the attitudes that support or undermine it. Papers name trust as a stated aim or evaluation dimension, and name mistrust — driven by privacy worries, incorrect output, or bias — as the condition to be addressed. The factor is the person's attitude, not the counterpart's reliability.
framing: BOTH. The corpus states trust as something to gain, improve, or measure, and also states mistrust as a persisting problem the design confronts.

definition: Whether a person's reliance on an automated counterpart matches how far it should be relied on in the case at hand. Papers frame the harm as accepting output without scrutiny, so the person's performance is capped by the system's, and frame the target capacity as appropriate or calibrated reliance. The subject is the person's disposition to accept, not the accuracy of what is being accepted.
framing: BOTH. The harm framing dominates (overreliance, unwarranted confidence, confirmation bias); the same papers state the paired capacity as "appropriate reliance" or appropriately calibrated trust.

definition: People systematically take the lower-effort option even when a more effortful one would serve them better, and papers treat this preference as a fixed condition any design must survive rather than something to argue against. The claimed harm is that convenience drives shallow engagement, over-disclosure, or effort minimization. It transplants to any setting where the easy path and the good path diverge.

human_factor: accountability and ethics of delegating judgment
definition: When a judgment that carries consequences for someone is handed to a machine, it becomes unclear who answers for the result, and whether handing it over was permissible at all. Papers frame this as clarifying responsibility across asymmetric parties, or as the ethical concerns practitioners raise about delegating an assessment. It transplants to any consequential decision a person could either make or pass on.

The person's grasp of content that is dense, technical, or outside their expertise — what it says, what it implies, and what matters in it. Papers frame the difficulty as arising from the material and the reader's distance from it, and frame comprehension as the human dimension the design engages. The object understood is subject matter, not machinery.
framing: BOTH. Comprehension is named as the capacity to support ("improve comprehension", "support code understanding") and its absence as the stated problem ("most people do not have the domain expertise", descriptions that "do not adequately describe important insights").

definition: The cost of finding the relevant material inside a large, fragmented, or linear body of sources before any work on it can begin. Papers frame this as manual scanning, sifting, or locating, and sometimes as the inverse capacity of encountering material one would not have thought to look for. It transplants to any corpus a person must get through to reach the few items that matter.

The person imposes structure on open-ended material whose organising shape is not given in advance, moving in branching, parallel cycles between gathering and interpreting. Papers claim their designs engage this structuring work, including the difficulty of pulling scattered material into a coherent account. What is at stake is the construction of an organisation, not the absorption of one already present in the material.
framing: CAPACITY — the corpus describes sensemaking, foraging, and narrative construction as the analytic and interpretive work people do, with its branching structure framed as resistant to automation rather than as a defect.

definition: Retrieval of specific past content — what was said, decided, done, or lived through — at the moment the person needs it. Papers claim their designs engage the difficulty of getting particular prior material back into mind, and in some cases the emotional cost of doing so. The object is content that existed earlier and must be brought back, not structure the person must currently hold.
framing: BOTH — the corpus states recall as a target to be raised (information recall, being reminded of overlooked material) and as a difficulty in its own right (rationale that cannot be recalled in real time, memories that are demanding to retrieve).

definition: The person's arrival at new understanding or new connections that were not stated anywhere in the material they were given. The claimed difficulty is that the person receives conclusions rather than being able to explore and draw their own, or that forming and validating candidate understandings across scattered material is costly. It transplants to any body of material a person is expected to learn something new from.

Within material the person already has in front of them, telling which elements carry the significance and which are incidental. The claimed difficulty is that significance is not marked in the artifact, so consequential detail goes unnoticed, particularly for those without the experience to know where to look. It transplants to any artifact whose important parts are not visually or structurally distinguished from its unimportant ones.

As a body of work grows, the person loses hold of its overall shape and drifts into local detail, unable to see how the parts relate or where they are within the whole. Papers claim their designs engage this loss of overview and orientation. The material is present and available; what fails is the person's grasp of its structure.
framing: DEFICIT/HARM — the corpus states this as difficulty and drift: hard to oversee a growing draft, hard to track how parts connect, tempting to revise locally, pushed toward implementation detail instead of the shape of the design.

definition: People make sense of what they are doing now by reaching backward into what has happened and forward into what might, and this looking across time is treated as work in its own right. The factor is the person's prospective and retrospective cognition — the construction of meaning and agency out of past and future — rather than the storage or retrieval of facts about either.

Working something out and telling someone about it make incompatible demands on the same material: the trace that supports discovery is messy in exactly the ways an audience-facing account must not be. The factor is the person's position between these two modes and the cost of converting the artifact of one into the artifact of the other. Papers frame it as a tension or gap rather than as a sequence of steps.

The person's claimed capacity to direct what an automated process does and to remain the one deciding, rather than receiving a result they did not shape. Papers state it as control, steering, autonomy, empowerment, or ownership of the decision, and state its absence as limited control or as automation encroaching on the person's role. It is about who holds the wheel, independent of what the output is.
framing: BOTH. The dominant framing is a CAPACITY to be served (control, ownership, efficacy, steering as something users want); the corpus also frames its loss as a harm — "limited user control", and "the tension between automation and scholarly agency".

human_factor: collaborative roles and the work left to the person
definition: A piece of work that the person could have done alone is split between them and a system, and the split settles what the person is left holding — which parts of the task stay theirs, and whether what stays is the part worth doing or the residue. The factor is the person's difficulty and capacity under that allocation: getting a share of the work that is meaningful to them, taking up whatever the system hands back, and covering whatever the split leaves uncovered. It transplants to any setting where part of a person's work is taken over by something else — a delegate, an assistant, an earlier generation of automation — and it is coded from claims about the person's portion, never from a description of how the system's own roles were configured.

An externally timed intrusion pulls a person out of ongoing work, or the work itself is fragmented across threads and contexts so that continuity is repeatedly broken. Papers claim their designs engage the cost of being taken out of flow and the risk that any offered help is intrusive. The trigger lies outside the person's own attentional effort, which is what makes this distinct from failing to stay focused.
framing: DEFICIT/HARM — every central assertion in the packet states this as a cost: disruption, intrusion, fragmentation, being pulled out of the workflow, or being sidelined.

definition: The claim that some part of a task rests on knowledge, context, or judgment that only the particular human holds, so automation can supplement but not stand in for them. Papers state it as tasks requiring human insight, as contextual knowledge an outsider or a machine lacks, and as augmentation rather than replacement. It is a claim about what the person uniquely contributes, not about a system's accuracy.
framing: CAPACITY. The human contribution is the thing being asserted and protected — domain knowledge, educational insight, expert interpretation, capability enhancement rather than replacement.

human_factor: shift in the human's role and practice
definition: When part of a person's work is taken over, what remains of their role is not simply less of the same but a different job, with different competences at its centre. The factor is this reallocation of what the person is there to do — the move from one mode of practice to another — as the dimension the paper says its design engages. It concerns the shape of the person's role, not their skill level within it.

An exchange that runs long enough, or resumes often enough, stops holding together: what was established earlier no longer bears on what happens now, and the person must re-establish ground they had already laid. The factor is the human's experience of coherence and completeness across an extended or multi-session engagement, and the burden of repair when that coherence lapses. It concerns the thread of the interaction, not the person's own memory.

Work that involves a slow-producing partner puts the person into stretches of dead time they must inhabit, not merely tolerate. The factor is the human experience of waiting — what the person does, feels, and attends to during a pause they did not choose and cannot shorten. It is the temporal experience on the person's side, not the duration figure itself.

Some reasoning tasks depend on what the person has not yet been told: the order of disclosure, and the withholding of certain facts until earned, is a precondition for the inference the person is trying to make. The factor is the person's dependence on paced, structured release of information, and the collapse of their reasoning when material arrives out of order or too early. It concerns the sequencing of what reaches the person, not the truth of it.

The person's capacity to turn attention back on themselves — their own process, decisions, feelings, or conduct — and to notice something about it they had not articulated. Papers claim designs engage this by provoking moments of reflection, replaying what the person did, or prompting inquiry rather than supplying answers. The object of attention is the person, not the material or the system.
framing: CAPACITY. Consistently framed as reflection to be supported, provoked, or made possible; the corpus does not frame it as a deficit.

definition: The person's capacity to question, examine, and weigh what is put in front of them rather than take it at face value. Papers claim designs invoke this by presenting alternative perspectives, by prompting reconsideration during reading, or by making a claim available for scrutiny. It is directed outward at content, claims, or the arrangement being examined.
framing: CAPACITY. Framed as a skill to invoke, build, or provoke — critical thinking, critical re-examination, reflective engagement.

definition: Whether a person encounters viewpoints other than the ones already available to them, and whether those viewpoints are preserved rather than collapsed. Papers frame the deficit as narrowing — echo chambers, polarization, lack of access to varied others — and the capacity as perspective expansion or considering alternate readings. It transplants to any setting where the range of positions a person meets shapes what they conclude.

The person's ability to judge accurately what they do and do not know, and to plan, monitor, and adjust their own effort on that basis. Papers claim their designs engage this second-order control over one's own learning, including the miscalibration — typically overconfidence — that undermines it. The object of judgment is the person's own state of knowing, not the material or the system.
framing: BOTH — the corpus names metacognition, self-regulation, and calibration as skills to be strengthened, and overconfidence and inability to plan one's own study as the deficits designs target.

human_factor: need for direction while stuck, and uptake of direction offered
definition: The person needs direction on how to proceed at the moment they are stuck, and whether they take up direction that is offered is itself variable. Papers claim their designs engage the absence of timely in-task support and the person's receptivity to it. The concern is being shown a way forward while working, not acquiring durable competence.
framing: BOTH — the corpus states absence of support as a deficit (lack of visual guidance, lack of timely help when confusion arises) and receptivity or uptake of guidance as a human disposition in its own right.

definition: The person cannot get sufficient purchase on their own work from the inside, and the outside judgment they need is scarce, slow, or unavailable at the moment of work. The factor is the standing demand for a critical second view on an artifact the person themselves produced, and the cost structure that keeps such a view from arriving when it would matter. Claimed by the authors as the human condition their design engages; not independently verified here.

A person's level of activation — felt as tension or stress — is treated as a dial that stands in a non-monotonic relation to how well they execute a task. The factor is that activation level together with its claimed consequences for performance, where too little and too much are each said to cost the person something. It concerns a modulated affective-physiological state, not the person's coping with adversity.

human_factor: acceptance and social perception of the agent
definition: People read a non-human counterpart in social terms — as warm or cold, competent or not, natural or stilted, a tool or an actor — and those readings govern whether they will have it around at all. Papers claim their designs engage this social attribution and the acceptance that follows from it. The dimension is the person's perceptual and attitudinal stance toward the counterpart, not their willingness to act on its outputs.
framing: BOTH — the corpus reports perceived anthropomorphism, warmth, and competence as dimensions to be raised, and robotic, unnatural, or discomforting impressions as the deficit designs address.

definition: Bonds between people are formed and maintained by sharing experience and being together in an activity, and their absence is felt as loneliness or isolation. Papers claim their designs engage this connection between people and the conditions that block or enable it. The relationship in question is human-to-human, even where a machine sits in the middle.
framing: BOTH — the corpus names connection, comfort, companionship, and shared creative engagement as goods, and loneliness and barriers to shared participation as the deficits designs address.

definition: The sense of being with other people, and the warmth, mutual awareness, and shared identity that build up between them. Papers frame the deficit as fragile early interaction, missing nonverbal cues, or an interface that pulls attention away from the group. It transplants to any mediated setting where people must feel co-present with one another to work or relate.

When part of what passes between two people was produced by something other than either of them, the exchange's standing as a genuine one comes into question — for the sender, the receiver, and the relationship. The factor is this concern about whether a mediated interaction still counts as authentic, and the reluctance or damage that attends it. It is a property of the interpersonal exchange, not of the text that carries it.

A person and a counterpart they are working with — another person or a system — hold different conceptions of the same thing, and the gap between those conceptions has to be closed for the work to proceed. The factor is the person's side of establishing that common ground: converging on a shared reference, adapting to the counterpart as it adapts to them, and fitting the counterpart's contributions into their own cognitive and creative process. The parties are mutually reachable and can negotiate meaning with each other, which is what distinguishes this from addressing a public; whether the counterpart is a person or a system does not bear on the coding, and difficulty of integrating a machine counterpart's contributions is evidence here on the same footing as miscommunication between two people.
framing: BOTH — the corpus names representational gaps, miscommunication, and expressive suppression as harms, and grounded communication, partnership, co-creativity, bidirectional alignment, and shared mental states as capacities the work depends on; integration difficulty is framed as what stands in the way of that capacity.

definition: Whether what a person produces lands with people who are not present during its production — whether it reaches them at all, holds them, and is taken the way it was meant. Papers claim their designs engage the producer's problem of anticipating and affecting an absent receiving public. The receivers are a body the producer cannot interrogate, which is what separates this from any face-to-face understanding problem.
framing: BOTH — the corpus frames reach and audience engagement as things to be raised, and audience misinterpretation and its societal consequences as a harm the producer must anticipate.

definition: One person's grasp of another person's inner state — their goals, feelings, or reading of a situation — when that state is not directly observable and must be inferred. Papers claim their designs engage both the inference itself and the affective response that follows it. The other party is a human whose perspective is the object of understanding, not a co-worker whose actions need coordinating.
framing: BOTH — the corpus names empathy and mutual understanding as capacities to be raised, and simultaneously names imagination gaps and misinterpretation of the other party as failures the design targets.

definition: Whether what a person says fits the relationship, the culture, and the moment, over and above being clear or well formed. The claimed demand is that fluency is not sufficient: an utterance must be calibrated to who is receiving it and what stands between them. It transplants to any communication addressed to a particular person in a particular relation.

How far a person is drawn into and absorbed by an experience rather than receiving it passively — engagement, immersion, presence, or felt involvement in the moment. Papers claim designs engage this by making the person an active participant or by deepening the sense of being inside the experience. It concerns absorption during the activity, not whether the person chose to start it or liked it afterwards.
framing: CAPACITY. Framed as something to foster, enhance, or evaluate — engagement, satisfaction and immersion, perceived presence, affective attachment.

definition: Whether a person wants to undertake and keep at an activity, and what they are pursuing through it. Papers claim their designs engage the drive to start and persist, including the underlying needs — autonomy, competence, relatedness — from which papers say that drive comes, and the mismatch when an activity's stated purpose is not the person's own. The factor is the wanting, prior to any question of ability.
framing: CAPACITY — the corpus states motivation as something to strengthen or raise: intrinsic motivation, intentions to practise, and the needs underpinning them.

definition: A person wants to conduct themselves differently from how they currently do, and cannot sustain the change against habit, ambivalence, and the states that drive the old conduct. Papers claim their designs engage both the entrenched pattern and the effort to move away from it. The object is the person's habitual conduct in life, not their use of the system in front of them.
framing: BOTH — the corpus names problematic, excessive, or mindless conduct as a harm the person themselves recognises, and behaviour change, perseverance, and mindfulness as capacities the design engages.

definition: Whether a person keeps coming back over weeks or months, when the benefit of an activity depends on repetition and the default trajectory is dropping off. The claimed difficulty is decline over time rather than the person's first encounter. It transplants to any activity whose value is only realized through sustained repeated participation.

The exclusion of some people from an activity that is available to others, and the claim that removing that exclusion is what a design exists to do. Papers state a gap in participation — content that cannot be perceived, communication that cannot be conducted — and frame the inequality between those who can and cannot take part as the problem. Following the handoff's rule, this is coded only where access for the excluded group is the entire point of the design, not wherever such a group appears as participants.
framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Stated as inaccessibility, a communication gap, no choice, and aggravated inequality between disabled and non-disabled people.

human_factor: translating between forms with conflicting norms
definition: The person must re-express material in a second form whose conventions contradict the first form's, while keeping whatever made the original worth having. The claimed difficulty is that satisfying the target form's demands actively violates the source form's norms or the person's own training. It transplants to any conversion between representations with incompatible standards of what counts as good.

The person acts with their body and inside the physical setting the work concerns, and papers claim this bodily, in-place engagement is part of how the work gets done. The claimed deficit is separation: doing the work at a remove from the material context strips out information and felt continuity the person was relying on. It transplants to any activity whose decisions depend on being bodily present where the result will live.

A person has to understand how a place is laid out and to picture arrangements and movements within it that are not in front of them. The factor is this spatial understanding and mental simulation — reading a layout, holding its structure, and imagining what could occupy or traverse it. It concerns reasoning about space, in any setting where spatial structure carries meaning.

When several people work on the same thing at the same time, they must divide labour, take turns, and adjust to each other's moves, and the quality of that meshing is itself at stake. The factor is the observable conduct of joint work between people — who does what, in what order, and how the group's strategy settles. It concerns behaviour among humans, whatever the task.

human_factor: minority voice and psychological safety in groups
definition: In a group where influence is unevenly distributed, holding a dissenting view and being able to say it are different things, and the second carries a social cost the first does not. The factor is whether a person in the weaker position feels safe enough to voice a divergent opinion, and the conformity and groupthink that follow when they do not. "Minority" here is a position in the group's power structure, not a demographic category.

When several people judge the same material, papers treat both their convergence and their non-convergence as things at stake: agreement is wanted, but agreement reached by influence rather than independent assessment is a loss. The factor is this two-sided tension over how much judges should move toward each other. It transplants to any setting where multiple people rate, label, or decide on shared items.

The person's act of putting inner states, interpretations, or personal experience into an externalised form for others or for themselves. Papers claim their designs engage the reach and depth of that act — whether the person manages to convey what they meant, and how they feel about having disclosed it. The factor is the expressive act and its subjective adequacy, not the quality of the resulting artifact.
framing: CAPACITY — the corpus presents expression and disclosure as human activities to be enabled or deepened (emotional expression, satisfaction with one's disclosure, expressing an interpretation), with vulnerability noted alongside rather than as the dominant framing.

definition: The person's worry about what of themselves they are giving away, and the tendency to reveal more than the task requires. Papers frame the difficulty as decisions that are numerous, context-dependent, and made without perceptible control over the trade-off between usefulness and exposure. The factor is the person's concern and disclosure behaviour, not any confidentiality property of the technology.
framing: BOTH. Predominantly a harm (over-disclosure, privacy concerns, being overwhelmed by the volume of decisions), with a paired capacity framing in claims about perceptible control, consent as a dynamic process, and data sovereignty.

definition: Whether a person regards a result as theirs — as something they made and deserve credit for — when an intermediary did part of the making. Papers claim their designs engage this felt authorship and the credit that attaches to it. The question is attribution and possession of the result, not how much of the process the person directed.
framing: BOTH — the corpus names declines in ownership and self-credit as harms, and a strengthened sense of authorship or directorial agency as a capacity designs engage.

definition: A person must assemble and put forward an account of who they are for others to read, and doing so is a construction task distinct from having the qualities being presented. The factor is that work of building and expressing a professional or personal identity to an audience. It concerns the presented self, whatever the medium in which it is presented.

human_factor: preservation of the person's own voice and expression
definition: A person's distinctive style, intention, or way of speaking can be flattened or suppressed when an intermediary reshapes what they produce. Papers claim their designs engage the survival of that individual character through the intermediary's involvement. What is at stake is the particularity of this person's expression, not who is credited for the result.
framing: DEFICIT/HARM — the corpus states this as loss: intention and voice only partially captured, personal characteristics displaced by generic output, self-censorship, and cultural norms locked in place by filtering.

definition: An action that works perfectly well in private becomes costly when bystanders can see or hear it, and the person declines to perform it rather than be seen doing so. The factor is this social cost of visible or audible interaction in the presence of others, and the resulting unavailability of otherwise workable ways of acting. It concerns how the person is perceived by others nearby, not what the others learn.

human_factor: originality and appropriation of existing work
definition: What a person produces with help may reproduce someone else's work or manner without their knowing it, exposing them to a charge they did not intend to incur. The factor is the person's exposure to and concern about unoriginality — recreating prior art, taking on another's style, or plagiarism — as a property of the work they will put their name to. It concerns the relation between the person's output and other people's existing work.

human_factor: awareness of bias, one's own and encoded
definition: Skew that is present but unnoticed — in the person's own assumptions, in the norms carried by the material they work with, or in the outputs they accept — and the difficulty of bringing it into view. Papers claim their designs engage noticing, prioritising, and reasoning about such skew. The factor is the person's awareness, not the existence of the skew.
framing: BOTH — the corpus states blind spots and overlooked biases as deficits, and recognition of bias, awareness of encoded norms, and fair representation as capacities the design engages.

definition: The labour a task costs a person, counted in time, repetition, tedium, or fatigue. The claim is that a person must expend more of themselves on the task than the task is worth, or that the expenditure is misallocated toward overhead. It is about the quantity of work demanded, not about how hard that work is to think through.
framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Consistently a burden to be reduced, shifted, or reallocated — "time-consuming and tedious", "burdensome", "survey fatigue", "administrative overhead".

definition: The mental processing a task demands of a person at once — holding material in mind, integrating scattered pieces, or working through more information than can be handled. Papers claim this demand degrades the quality of what people do or crowds out the judgment they should be spending attention on. It is about processing demand, not about elapsed time or missing training.
framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Uniformly stated as load to be lowered, overload to be relieved, or burden that degrades response quality.

definition: How fast and how well the work gets done — throughput, speed of producing an artifact, and measured quality of performance on the task. The factor covers both units to which that outcome is attributed: the individual person's own speed and quality at their own task, and the joint result produced by a person and a system working together where the paper treats the outcome as a property of the pairing rather than of either party alone. Both readings are coded here, and which one is at issue is read off the paper's own attribution; the joint reading additionally requires a claim about the pairing, such as that neither the person's skill nor the system's standalone accuracy predicts the joint outcome. Papers claim their designs engage this as the headline human dimension, stated in terms of the process being sped up or the performance being better. The factor is the observable performance of the work, not the person's felt exertion in doing it.
framing: CAPACITY — the corpus states this as a gain to be had (efficiency, speed, versatility, human performance), with slowness framed as the limitation of existing tooling.

definition: What it costs the person to work the thing: how much effort goes into figuring out what to do, how fluently the action they intend becomes the action the system takes, and how satisfied they are with the doing of it. The factor is the person's experience of operating an instrument — the same difficulty anyone has driving an unfamiliar machine — and it transplants to any operable artifact, with or without a model behind it. It is coded only from claims about what the person experienced or reported; a designer's assertion that the interface is simple is not evidence for it, and neither is any property attributed to the artifact rather than to the person using it.

A finite attentional resource has to be directed at what matters and sustained there, across competing demands and against declining alertness. Papers claim their designs engage the allocation of attention, the drift away from the target, and the alertness the person can hold over time. The concern is the person's ongoing attentional state, whatever is competing for it.
framing: BOTH — the corpus states distraction, divided attention, and fatigue-impaired alertness as deficits, and attentiveness to content and low attentional demand as properties to be raised or protected.

definition: The claim that a task demands training, proficiency, or specialist judgment that the intended person does not have, so the task is closed to them or done worse. It covers steep learning curves, tools built for specialists, and stated gaps between novices and experts. The person's competence, not the interface's clarity, is what the paper says is missing.
framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Stated as a lack, a steep curve, an exclusion, or a gap between novice and expert performance.

definition: The person's acquisition of knowledge, skill, or practice that they carry away from the interaction. Papers claim designs engage this by giving examples, feedback, simulated practice, or exposure to how others do the task, and some claim it as something a design must be careful not to supplant. What distinguishes it is that the person is meant to end up more capable, not merely to have finished the task.
framing: CAPACITY. Stated as learning gains, learning outcomes, learning strategies, or learning to be protected from short-circuiting.

definition: The person's belief in their own ability to do the thing, and their confidence in the judgments they reach. Papers frame the deficit as a felt sense of failure or low perceived competence that keeps people from attempting or persisting, and the capacity as confidence to approach a task or to commit to a decision. It is a belief about oneself, not about a system.
framing: BOTH. Deficit framings (sense of failure, low self-efficacy, low perceived competence as a demotivating factor) sit alongside capacity framings (confidence to approach, updating one's own judgment with higher confidence).

definition: The felt quality of the experience for the person — whether it lands as enjoyable, moving, visceral, or by contrast as flat and desensitized. Papers claim the design engages the affective register of the encounter itself, not the person's task outcome. It transplants to any artifact whose worth is stated partly in how it feels to receive it.

The affective cost a person bears from being exposed to, or having to engage with, emotionally heavy material or events. Papers frame this as distress, overwhelm, frustration, vulnerability, or emotional harm that accumulates on the person and can drive them out of the activity. It transplants to any setting where sustained emotional exposure is part of the work or the encounter.

The person is under a stressor they experience as taxing, and the factor covers both the felt stress itself and their capacity to appraise and cope with it. Papers claim to engage the stressor, the appraisal, the coping response, or the person's sense of control over a situation they cannot structurally change. Transplants to any setting where a person must carry on under demand they did not choose.

human_factor: exposure to harm from acting on generated output
definition: The person stands to be hurt, or to hurt something they care about, if they act on what the system produced. Papers frame the human dimension as the exposure the person carries and must guard against — physical breakage, psychological injury, an unacceptable output reaching a vulnerable recipient. It transplants to any setting where acting on an automated suggestion has consequences the person cannot undo.

human_factor: unawareness of a harm until too late
definition: A consequence of the person's own activity is invisible or unfamiliar at the moment of acting, so it cannot enter their decision until after the fact. Papers frame the target as raising awareness of a harm, cost, or risk the population is said not to know about. It transplants to any setting where the effect of an action is displaced in time, scale, or visibility from the action itself.

People make mistakes and lapse in attention while acting, and in some settings a mistake injures someone or breaks something. The factor is the person's own error-proneness and the bodily or operational consequence attached to it. It transplants to any activity where a slip by the person has a cost beyond needing to redo the step.

Beyond doing the work, a person must produce an artifact whose function is to prove to a supervising party that the work was done to requirement. The factor is that second, documentary obligation and the labour it adds — an artifact shaped by an auditor's demands rather than by the task's own needs. It concerns answering to an authority, not the difficulty of the underlying task.

human_factor: independence and quality of life in daily living
definition: A person's ability to carry out the ordinary activities of their own life without depending on another person, and the standard of living that follows from it. Papers frame the target as relief from repeated manual effort in everyday tasks or as quality-of-life gains in daily and leisure activity. It transplants to any setting where the stake is a person conducting their own life rather than completing an assigned task.
